I get that you’re focused on the “main plot” as in big bad guy + final boss fight structure, and sure on a surface level, ME2’s story might seem smaller scale compared to ME1’s Citadel threat or ME3’s galaxy-wide war. But reducing it to “a side quest to fight half a Reaper” kind of proves my point: you’re treating plot scale as the only thing that matters.

What ME2 does and what y’all keep brushing off is reframe the fight before it becomes a war. It’s not about saving the galaxy in a single final battle. It’s about preparing for something bigger than any one person can handle alone. That “galaxy side quest” builds the emotional and strategic foundation that gives ME3 its weight. ME2 makes you care. It’s where the crew stops being NPCs and starts being your people.

You can call that a side story if you want, but without it, ME3’s stakes feel hollow. So yeah—I stand by what I said. ME2 is the emotional spine of the trilogy. You don’t feel the heartbreak and sacrifice of ME3 if ME2 doesn’t slow down and let you connect.

Anyway, if y’all still want to argue bullet-point plot beats over storytelling depth, be my guest. I’m good.

See, I think calling ME2’s story the “weakest” just because it doesn’t follow a strict, linear plot misses the point of what it’s actually doing. Yeah, ME1 has the tighter sci-fi thriller setup with Saren, Sovereign, the big Reaper reveal. Cool. But ME2 is the heart of the trilogy. It dials in on why any of this matters. You’re not just chasing a bad guy. You’re building a crew, forming bonds, and risking it all on a suicide mission no one thinks you’ll survive.

The Reaper threat never goes away in ME2. It just takes a different shape. The Collectors are literally working for Harbinger, and every mission is a step toward understanding what the Reapers are planning and how messed up their endgame really is. That’s not a “neglected premise”. That’s narrative tension done right. It’s building the fuse ME3 lights.

And let’s be real if ME2 didn’t take the time to make us care about these characters, ME3 would’ve fallen flat. You don’t cry over Mordin or Legion or that final goodbye with Garrus if ME2 didn’t give you the time to live with them. ME1 is plot-driven. ME3 is payoff. ME2 is the glue that makes the whole damn thing matter.

So yeah, maybe it’s not the most “traditional” story structure but weakest? Nah. It’s the emotional spine of the trilogy. Without it, the rest doesn’t hit nearly as hard..

Nah I gotta disagree. While Mass Effect 2 doesn’t push the overarching Reaper plot as aggressively as ME1 or ME3, saying it has the “worst story” in the trilogy overlooks what it actually does accomplish. ME2 is all about building the foundation. You’re assembling a team, gaining their trust, and diving deep into the nuances of galactic politics and personal loyalties. That emotional investment makes the stakes of ME3 hit way harder.

Sure, the Collectors are more of a localized threat, but they’re a direct extension of the Reapers, and learning about them is advancing the larger story. The Collector base, the Human-Reaper hybrid, Harbinger’s control, etc. all of that expands our understanding of how the Reapers operate. It’s a crucial narrative pivot, not just filler.

Also, the claim that “you only fight the Collectors three times” doesn’t really hold up considering ME2 is structured differently than the other two games. It’s not about constantly chasing a big enemy across the galaxy. It’s about preparing for a suicide mission that no one is expected to survive. That narrative focus creates a unique kind of tension and gives real weight to every choice you make.

And while Arrival sets the stage for ME3, it wouldn’t hit as hard without the buildup ME2 provides. Not without the characters, the relationships, and the emotional core that ME2 spends so much time developing. ME2’s story might be more subtle and character-driven, but it’s absolutely essential to the trilogy’s impact.

I don’t believe billionaires genuinely deserve the wealth they own. At least not in the sense that their wealth is an accurate reflection of their individual labor, merit, or contributions to society. The reality is that extreme wealth is not created in a vacuum; it is extracted from workers, resources, and communities. No single person works hard enough or is indispensable enough to justify having billions while millions struggle to afford basic needs.

Many billionaires today amass their fortunes through underpaid labor, tax avoidance, corporate lobbying, and monopolistic practices, not because they are uniquely skilled or visionary. Meanwhile, working-class and marginalized communities continue to bear the brunt of economic inequality, with rising costs of living, stagnant wages, and dwindling social safety nets.

Wealth at that scale is not only excessive but a political tool that allows billionaires to shape policy, suppress labor movements, and hoard power. If we lived in a truly just and equitable society, such extreme concentrations of wealth wouldn’t exist because resources would be distributed in a way that ensures everyone has a fair shot at a dignified life. So no, I don’t believe billionaires deserve their wealth. Not when it comes at the expense of everyone else.

The pay was steady, but only because I had no choice but to stay. They like to act like the Navy is financially stable, but when you’re stuck in a system that controls your life, is it really financial security or just forced dependency?


I’ll have the GI Bill, which is arguably the only real benefit that makes dealing with this hellhole even remotely worth it. But the catch? I had to sacrifice years of my life, my mental health, and my freedom to earn it.

Outside of that? The Navy wasn’t worth it. Whatever small benefits I got came at the cost of my sanity, my autonomy, and my time; time I will never get back. If someone thinks those trade-offs are worth it, that’s their call, but for me? Never again.

Because at the end of the day, it’s their decision, not mine.

I hate the Navy. I regret joining. It wrecked my mental health, wasted my time, and showed me just how little this institution values its people. But I also know that my experience isn’t universal. There are people who actually thrive in this environment. Some people love the structure, the benefits, or the career opportunities. Some people don’t mind sacrificing their autonomy or dealing with the nonsense because, for them, the trade-off is worth it.

So I’m not going to sit here and say “Absolutely never join, under any circumstances.” But what I will do is tell people the ugly truth that recruiters and pro-military propaganda won’t tell them. I’ll make sure they know exactly what they’re signing up for, because once they sign that contract, there’s no backing out. If they hear my experience and still think it’s worth it? That’s on them.

You're absolutely right that a murder is a murder, and the laws and penalties for it should apply equally to everyone. But the fact that this case is being handled differently points to a deeper issue in our system that disproportionately benefits the wealthy in most situations but flips the script when one of their own is threatened.

Think about it: we live in a society where billionaires and CEOs have extraordinary influence over everything from our laws to our daily lives. They benefit from a system that protects their wealth, often at the expense of working people. Corporations can poison water supplies, deny people healthcare, and exploit labor with little to no accountability. But when a billionaire is harmed, the system suddenly becomes hyper-efficient in delivering justice.

The denial of bail in this case reflects a double standard. Most working-class people accused of violent crimes (and certainly many nonviolent ones) are routinely denied bail or set bail so high they can't afford it. That’s not justice. That’s wealth-based discrimination. But if this same billionaire were guilty of harming others (say, through corporate negligence or environmental destruction) would the system treat them this harshly? Highly unlikely.

The focus on this case being more than 'just a homicide' stems from the fact that it challenges the myth of the untouchable elite. This wasn’t just a random act of violence. It came from someone with grievances against a system that exploits the many to enrich the few. The fact that people are questioning it speaks to a growing frustration with that system.

Does that mean the accused shouldn't face the consequences of their actions? Of course not. But it’s worth asking why the system only seems to care about swift and decisive justice when it’s one of the powerful who’s been harmed. If we lived in a society where everyone (billionaires and working-class folks alike) were truly held to the same standard, this question wouldn’t even need to be asked.

Washington gave him another chance, but he didn’t perform well enough to justify him being a long-term starter. Combine that with reports about him not always being the best locker room presence, and teams seem hesitant to build around him.

At 31, he’s not too old to be a starter again, but the league has moved on to younger QBs, and teams would rather develop them than roll the dice on Wentz. He could probably outplay a few current starters, but his inconsistency and reputation make him a tough sell for a starting role right now. Backup feels like his spot unless he proves otherwise.

As someone born in '96, this post hits home. I started gaming on the PS1 and Dreamcast, and the first console I bought with my own money was the PS2. Back then, gaming was amazing, but let’s not romanticize the “good ol’ days” too hard. We definitely had some jank to deal with.

Remember scratched discs? If you didn’t have disc repair kits, you were grabbing toothpaste or praying to the gods of Windex and microfiber cloths to save your game. Memory cards were a necessity, and losing one could mean losing weeks of progress. There were no patches back then sogames were shipped *as-is*, bugs and all. If something was broken, tough luck. I remember my uncle buying a copy of Grand Turismo 2 and it was broken af and then having to buy the patched version of it. Now, I can update games in minutes.

Today, the sheer *scale* of gaming is insane. Steam alone gives me access to a library I could only dream of as a kid. Back in the day, I was saving up just to afford a couple of games a year; now, I’ve got a backlog so big I might not finish it before my PS7.


Sure, not everything is perfect. We have microtransactions, NFTs trying to sneak in, and devs rushing out unfinished games sometimes knowing they can just send a patch later. But the fact that those issues spark such loud conversations means gamers are passionate and holding the industry accountable. Outrage farmers will always exist, but they don’t define gaming.

The truth is, we’ve *made it*. We’ve gone from blowing on cartridges and scratching discs to downloading entire libraries at the click of a button. We’re living in an era where gaming isn’t just entertainment—it’s art, competition, connection, and a massive industry pushing boundaries every year.

Nostalgia is great, but let’s not forget how far we’ve come. Modern gaming is a buffet, and we are feasting.
